January 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 3
“I have gotten so much from the Guild that I feel I
need to give something back.” This is a recent comment from one of our members. This warms my
heart along with all of the other volunteers that put
in sweat and time to organize, plan, and run our
Guild!
Please join me to welcome Donna Rhindress as our
new WIT Liaison. Donna lives on The Misty Isles,
Haida Gwaii, but is easily contacted via email and
telephone. We do not publish phone numbers
online but her email is wit@gvwg.ca.
I am also delighted, and relieved, that Dustin Cook
has returned as our Visiting Demonstrator Coordinator. Dustin is a genuine connector and regular
attendee of at least two symposia, an excellent organizer of group dinners, so he is perfect for that
role.
Speaking of volunteers, we have a need for someone to be a greeter. The role is simple and most of
all fun. All you do is attend the monthly in person
meeting from 06:30 and look for new faces entering the Hall and introduce them to the Guild. We
have a nice document to hand to people as a guide.
This volunteer role can be SHARED with others, but
it really needs someone to make sure there is at
least one greeter at each meeting. If you like talking
with people, you are fully qualified to take this on!
We had another great turnout last month! Thank
you to Pippa Lattey for an inspiring and innovative
demo on making pill boxes from those tiny and precious cut-offs that we lovingly save… but until now
did not know what to do with.
February’s president’s challenge is “captivity”
“Many hands make for small work.”
Steve

Happy New Year everyone! Hope you all had a
restful holiday and were able to spend some quality time in front of your lathe.
We start this month’s newsletter with some valuable information about the guild’s 2025 Introduction
to Woodturning classes (formerly Turning 101) followed by an article by Larry Stevenson on the creative process behind his Celtic Knot Bowl featured
on this month’s cover.
First time contributor Rob Fahlman, a relatively
new member, tells us about his introduction to
woodturning and subsequent journey down that
slippery slope.
This month’s Member Profile features Pippa Lattey,
a talented artist and turner who was also our featured speaker at our last meeting in November.
As always, we need more material for our newsletter so please keep those articles coming. All
submissions can be emailed to editor@gvwg.ca
Steve

January 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 4
The Guild is happy to announce that Introduction
to Woodturning classes for 2025 will commence at
the end of February on the following dates.
Introduction to Bowl Turning
Dates: Sat 22nd & Sun 23rd Feb and Sat 1st Mar
Cost: $150
Instructor: Claudia Hayward
This 3-day course focuses on teaching the basic
techniques for bowl turning including:
•
the principal tools used for bowl turning and
how to sharpen them.
•
alternative ways for preparing and mounting
bowl blanks on a lathe
•
cuts used to shape the outside and inside of
bowls
Introduction to Spindle Turning
Dates: Sat 3rd & Sun 4th May * these dates are
tentative and may be subject to change pending
Ed’s availability
Cost: $100
Instructor: Ed Pretty
This 2-day course focused on teaching the basic
techniques for spindle turning or turning between
centers. You will be introduced to:
•
the principal tools used for spindle turning and
how to sharpen them, in particular the spindle
roughing gouge, skew chisel, spindle gouge &
parting tool.
•
alternative ways for preparing and mounting
spindle blanks on a lathe.
•
cuts used to create the primary shapes that appear in spindle work, in particular beads &
coves.
Neither course is intended to be a project course,
so you won’t make anything specifically other than
lots of wood shaving. The key takeaways are intended to be knowledge and tool handling skills
that you can take back to your own shop to turn
safely and with confidence.
For more information and to register please email
peterhill64@telus.net

January 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 5
Have you ever had an idea of something that you
would like to create, but have no idea how to do it?
Do these thoughts keep recurring in your brain and
you keep pushing them down thinking that you do
not have the skills to produce this idea? Well, I do
too! Sometimes I do not want to share these
thoughts with another woodturner, as I do not
want to lose control of this idea and have someone
else realize my dreams. I believe these things happen to all of us and the realization of this spurred
me on to write this article with a recent story to
back it up.
When I reflect on all of the demonstrations that I
have attended over the years I have been involved
with the Greater Vancouver Woodturners Guild,
and the AAW, the ones that have had the greatest
impact on me are the ones where the presenter
has taken on unfamiliar ground and had to overcome obstacles to realize their vision. New work,
cutting edge, whatever title you want to come up
with, these are the things that excite me. I just
never saw myself as having what it takes to produce these pieces, until now.
Let’s start the story. In 2019, just before Covid, our
guild was privileged to have Sharon Doughtie
demonstrate and teach classes at our guild. I have
always admired her work and was excited to
attend. Sharon demonstration was centered on
her Celtic Knot designed pieces. She was explaining how to layout these designs on a project when I
had a thought. Now, I have a brain that could be
considered a blessing or a curse, depending on
your viewpoint, as it never stops talking to me. I
put up my hand and asked if she had ever considered that once she had the design laid out, to get
rid of all the wood and just work on the knot. I
shall never forget her response, she looked at me
and said “Larry, I will leave that up to you”. To top
it off she had a very mischievous smile on her face.
That statement and the look on her face is engrained in my memory and it is just like she said it
yesterday. How does one respond to that? My
initial thought was to file it away and ruminate
over it later. This incident never left my brain for
very long and kept coming back and eventually my
thought was “Well, you opened your big mouth,
now is time to do something about it.”
When the dreaded Covid era was opening up I decided that I need to put this into a project. So firstly
I had to formulate a plan. I decided on bowl design, something I thought would be fairly simple, or
so I thought. I set up 3 criteria:
1. The wood must me fairly soft as there is going to be a lot of carving involved
2. I want the foot to be hidden as to not interfere with the design
3. I want the texture to emphasize the over and
under weave design.
Other than that I had no idea of the obstacles that
faced me in carrying this out. Firstly I had to come
up with a design. I have two books on Celtic designs and I scoured those and the internet to find a
design that could be laid out within a bowl. This is
the design that I selected in Figure 1.
It didn’t seem that difficult, or so I thought.
Before I go on there is a
quote that came into my
life in the 80’s that has
been very important to
me and guided and assisted me in moving
ahead in life against insurmountable odds that
I would like to share
with you.
“Until one is committed there is hesitancy, the
chance to draw back, always ineffectiveness. Concerning all acts of initiative or creation, there is one
elementary truth...that the moment one definitely
commits oneself, then Providence moves too. All
(Continued on page 6)
Figure 1

January 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 6
sorts of things occur to help one that would otherwise never have occurred. A whole stream of events
issues from the decision, raising in one’s favor all
manner of incidents and meetings and material assistance which no man would have believed would
have come his way.
Whatever you think you can do or believe you can
do, begin it. Action has magic, grace, and power in
it.”
― W.H. Murray - The Scottish Himalayan Expedition
OK, onward. I knew that I was totally committed to
seeing this project through and did realize that I
would face obstacles along the way and would
have to deal with them. I rummaged through my
roughed out bowl stash and found an alder bowl.
Perfect, easy to work with and easy to carve. Once
the bowl was trued up by turning it a second time
now I needed to do the layout. Here it is in in Figure 2.
I laid out a grid on the bowl into 48 segments and
10 radially to assist me in laying out the design.
Easier said than done. I tried various tapes but
none allowed me to do this as they didn’t stick well
enough to the wood and I didn’t want to apply a
finish that would assist in the tape sticking. It was
back to sketching out the pattern by using the grid
for guidance. Have a good look at the design and
you will notice that it isn’t symmetrical and this did
cause some problems. Now that I had the design
on the bowl I needed to remove all the negative
space. I drilled holes and then used a micromotor
with a drywall zip cutter to do this. It was grabby
and a pain. After all this was done I watched Andi
Wolfe do a presentation at the AAW in Portland
last June and learned that there is a better tool to
do this. It is called a 2 piece Mini Saw Drill Set
3/32, and 1/8 and is available from Woodcarver
Supply. I do own them now. Andi, where were you
when I needed you? Here is the roughed out bowl
in Figure 3.
Now all the work begins. I needed to take care to
only remove the unwanted wood to show the over
and under nature of the design, and not screw up
and ruin the entire piece, no pressure whatsoever.
I went over the entire bowl both sides drawing in
where some part was an over or an under and
checked and double and triple checked as this was
critical. You may notice that I have kept the wood
at 4 points along the rim and left this connected
(Continued from page 5)
(Continued on page 7)
Figure 2
Figure 3

January 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 7
until all the wood removal was done, as it provided
support to the entire piece.
This is when I discovered that wood removal with a
micromotor was a pain on the inside of the bowl.
The handle and cord get in the way much of the
time and you need to be a contortionist to perform
many of these processes. Every time I ran into an
obstacle, I would see that grin on Sharon’s face and
have to imagine that she tried this and ran into the
same obstacles. All part of the journey. Once all of
this carving and sanding was done and my life was
wasting away I was left with this, Figure 4.
Now I was faced with how to finish the piece off to
show it off as currently it didn’t look like I had
spent the many, many hours on it that I had. I tried
many different textures on pieces of alder as I
wanted to see the texture on the same wood. I
consulted with Art Liestman as he is a close friend.
He was very helpful and encouraging and offered
some sound advice on the progress of this piece. I
couldn’t decide on a specific texture but wanted to
ensure that my goal of the emphasis on the over
and under elements was realized. I walked away as
I needed a break from it.
Our guild recently celebrated our 25th anniversary
and we were privileged to have Michael Hosaluk
come and be our guest presenter. I applied to the
bingo draw to be able to attend one of his classes
and was fortunate enough to be drawn to attend.
He is a marvelous teacher and so much fun. I took
the unfinished piece to his class for critique and to
discuss texture. I told him my thoughts on what I
wanted to do and he said that I was complicating it
too much. He had a suggestion and I modified it
slightly and came up with the texture that I currently have. I practiced on a figure 8 piece so I
could have a physical representation of what I intended to do. This is Figure 5.
Hours of pyrography later I was closing in on the
final piece. Here is a picture along the way. Figure
6
The piece still required much work as I wanted to
be able to see the original wood as an element of
the texture. While doing this I came across a very
annoying issue, something I called Molecular Car-
(Continued from page 6)
(Continued on page 8)
Figure 4
Figure 5
Figure 6

January 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 8
bon Migration. Sound impressive, don’t you think.
When I was spraying Krylon Matte finish over the
piece, and yes the piece was thoroughly blown off
with compressed air, carbon migrated out of the
burnt grooves and obliterated the view of the unfinished wood. The solution required resanding
the surface many times and applying finish in very
light coats to not give any carbon molecules
enough medium to migrate into. Finally the piece
was finished and now time to sign. Notice that the
standoffs that I incorporated into the base do not
appear as obvious when you look from the top.
Figures 7, 8 and 9.
My point in writing this article isn’t a “How To” but
more of a “You Can Too”. We all have the ability to
do something far beyond what we think we can. I
have gotten a lot of “How many hours did that take
you?” I have discussed this with friends and I understand that if you are selling your pieces, this is
critical in coming up with a price. I am retired and
don’t rely on income from woodturning to live and
for that I am grateful, however I believe that there
is magnificence in all of us waiting to be shown,
that we can’t always consider “How Long?” some
piece took us to achieve. Whether you spend 250
hours on 1 piece or 250 hours on 25 pieces, you
have still spent 250 hours doing something that
you enjoyed and for that you should be grateful for
that opportunity. I would encourage everyone to
try and do something that you think is impossible
for you to do. You may be surprised at what you
can produce. You will definitely learn so much
along the journey.
In conclusion, I am so thankful for my interaction
with Sharon Doughtie for without her mischievous
smile and her answer to my original question this
piece may never have been made. I want to dedicate this piece in her honor, thanks Sharon.
(Continued from page 7)
Figure 7
Figure 8
Figure 9

January 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 9
Hello everyone.
During the 25th Anniversary Meeting, the Guild
celebrated a group of friends that had come together to create a community. The displays of
artistry were fantastic in their creativity, with many
of them seeming to defy the laws of nature. It was
inspirational to view these works of art and to
know I sat in the room with brilliance that could
both conceptualize these works of art and to turn
them into reality. The humble stories of friendship
and creativity moved me.
One of the sad notes that struck me, was the plea
for new members to step up.
I am one of the first to admit that I am relatively
new to the group. I don’t often bring pieces for
display. I don’t have much spare time these days
for turning, or much else. On the other hand, the
call to action moved me to try to contribute an article for the newsletter.
The article is entitled “My Origin Story”, because
every hero and every villain has a genesis. I wanted
to share why I spend time with my lathe and how I
came to this point.
The first time I had set eyes upon a lathe was back
in grade 8 shop class. That was a long time
ago. For those of you who might be counting, it
was during the later part of the last millennium.
I still remember my first project, a bat. Well to be
honest, it was more like a log that had the bark removed and some light sanding. It was definitely
worthy of the fire pit.
Fast forward around 25 years, during which life had
moved me to various parts of Western Canada,
where each move required me to be able to load
my entire world into a U-haul to set up in another
location. During this time both my family and my
amount of stuff grew. Each move needed a larger
truck.
The next time I touched a lathe was about 12 years
ago. I had seen a workshop posted at a tool-store
on a Saturday. Having young kids at the time, I
needed a break for my sanity. After some negotiations with my wonderful wife, I was able to spring
myself free for the Saturday and happily headed
out to the workshop.
Upon completion, I was delighted to walk away
with two pens and a sense of satisfaction and contentment.
Fast forward about seven years again, and that is
when the real addiction started….
My daughters we were in their teen years, my career was very busy, my wife's career was also very
busy. Time to myself seemed like a passing dream
that was slipping away. I realized, if I didn’t carve
time out specifically for myself, I would be swept
away by life and work, and lose who I am.
One Christmas, my loving wife bought me my first
small lathe. I was delighted and eagerly went
about deciding where to set it up.
Quickly I realized that this was not a “dining room
hobby”. Turning required space and space to make
a mess.
The spring finally rolled around, and I bounced out
of bed one weekend morning eager to set my lathe
up on an old table outside and get started. I had
spent the rest of the winter reading up on turning, I
had my pen blanks all set up, I had purchased my
first set of tools (more on that later) and with that I
headed outside.
From the moment I turned on my lathe, I knew I
was hooked. The speed of the wood that was spinning, the feel of the face mask, the tools in my
hand, it all felt perfect.
The crowning joy was when I first put tool to
wood. I will never forget that first spray of sawdust. Being engulfed with this was a feeling of elation.
To be honest, I am somewhat surprised I survived. My tools were out of the box and not
properly sharpened, my lathe had some bounce
(Continued on page 10)

January 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 10
and my lack of skills required me to do much more
sanding than turning, but I didn’t care. I walked
away from an entire day at the lathe, with my first
pen from my own equipment. I was on top of the
world.
These days, I have added many, many, many more
tools to my collection. I can’t pass a tool store
without spending a half hour or so looking around
to see if there is a new tool or an exceptional piece
of wood I need. I have trouble passing a fallen tree
or pile of wood without gazing just a little too long.
But I am sure I am the only one, right?
I still get a secret thrill each time I put a tool to
wood. I also have a sense of satisfaction and contentment at the end of the day, when I can come in
and show my latest triumph.
My work doesn’t compare to other Guild members,
but I don’t do this for others, I do this for me.
Wood turning brings me focus. As some of you
might know, one momentary lapse in concentration, can lead to a sharp reminder. Turning also
connects me with who I am. My mother was a hobby potter and my father worked with wood. Wood
turning gives me a connection to who I was and to
who I am.
Thank you for reading my story.
Here is a picture of my set up:
Until next time, keep your tools sharp and your
wits sharper.

January 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 11
Tell us about your background – how did you
get into woodturning?
I’m an artist, making mostly sculpture and 3D objects. My sculptures often move, or make sound or
light. I show in galleries, and I’ve created a few permanent outdoor public artworks. I use whatever
materials I can get my hands on: steel, wood, plastic, junk I find in the street, or fallen branches I find
in the park. Often the source of the material becomes a story that influences the final piece. For
example, I made a sculpture from a piano that I
inherited from local artist and musician Al Neil. I
rotated it upside down and made sound come out
of it. The piano spent decades in a cabin on the
shore of Burrard Inlet, so I wrote software to orchestrate the movements using local tide patterns.
The piano rests on a steel frame I welded myself
and rolls around on wheels I turned of UHMW plastic.
I got hooked on woodturning in art school, first at
Langara College and then at Emily Carr University
of Art + Design. I had some instruction, and then I
spent many hours playing around on the lathes.
Finally, five years after I graduated, I had the space
and time to start turning again. I started turning in
my own studio and joined the GVWG in the summer of 2021.
Tell us about your workshop/studio
I rent space in a shared artist studio building. I try
to reconfigure my studio to make room for my current projects and obsessions, and I have a lot of
collected materials: electronics, plastic junk, rope,
wire, and a growing pile of wood. The studio building has a shared mitre saw and drill press, and a
backyard with an outdoor “messy” workspace.
My lathe is an old Oneway 1224 that I bought from
Bob Burke in August 2022, along with a collection
of his accessories and tools. I added a skirt to keep
shavings out of the bottom, retractable wheels,
and cork tiles on the surface under the bed. I also
sewed a big canvas tool roll that hangs behind the
lathe.
What tools do you most like using on your
lathe?
I love having a collection of tools and picking out
the right one for the job.
For spindle work, I enjoy using a big skew.
For faceplate work, I like a swept back bowl gouge
and a chunky beading and parting tool.
I also enjoy using a Jacob’s chuck with a big old Forstener bit.
What is your favorite wood?
Anything local, and almost anything that's free...
but I am getting more selective as I gain experience
(Continued on page 12)

January 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 12
and as my wood collection grows.
I have a soft spot for Arbutus, because it's such a
beautiful tree, and an emblem of the west coast. I
love it with cracks and varied colours. I also enjoy
Big Leaf Maple, figured, spalted or otherwise. I
have turned quite a lot of Douglas Fir, mostly from
2x6 offcuts. Though it is a challenge to get a nice
finish, its worth it for that big thick corduroy grain,
and I love burning it to get a strong textured finish.
What finishes do you prefer using?
I like basic oils and waxes. I use paste wax if I want
to keep the raw colour, or Tung oil to bring out the
details in the wood. I like Tried and True Original
(linseed oil and beeswax) for bowls and kitchen
utensils. I sometimes use milk paint.
Do you ever incorporate other materials into
your pieces?
I like to combine turned wood with a found object
that is round, like a plastic lid. I have added LEDs to
some pieces, and also inlaid brass and copper wire.
What other types of woodworking or pursuits
do you have?
I have built a few Aeolian harps (wind-activated
harps) with my partner, musician Thomas Evdokimoff. Our latest one is made from red and yellow
cedar.
I've also been experimenting with basket weaving,
made from garden waste material and recycled
junk, along with my artist collective, "ad hoc plots".
We are doing some workshops in the next few
months in Burnaby at an amazing portable art studio
called
FLEET:
Edmonds
(https://
www.fleetstudios.org/program/visiting-artistadhoc-plots-collective).
What inspires you – where do you get your
ideas from?
I get ideas from the urban environment, and from
the natural environment too. I observe shapes, colours, movements, sound and light. I appreciate
good design, and I enjoy thinking about how functionality and form compliment one another. That’s
something that comes up in woodturning a lot.
I think a lot about systems, about invisible connections between different parts of our world. I think
about things that collect, and when they are discarded, where they end up. One of the most exciting things about being an artist is being allowed
to be curious and ask crazy questions, without ever
needing to answer those questions in any
straightforward or logical way.
(Continued from page 11)
(Continued on page 13)

January 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 13
Ideas can grow out of collaborations and conversations with other creative people. As a maker, I am
motivated by learning new skills, and finding new
materials. I love the feeling when I learn about
something new, and I can’t wait to find a project to
put it into.
Where do you usually display and/or sell your
work?
I show my art in galleries from time to time, and
sometimes in the Eastside Culture Crawl. I am
starting to think about selling my turnings, but I am
not quite there yet.
What is your favorite project to date?
I like making items that I can use every day. My favourites are two porridge bowls. I made the first
one for myself, from a pear bowl blank I won in
Barry Wilkinson’s raffle last year. I inset brass into a
little void, which makes a nice highlight. I made a
second, larger bowl for my partner from some kind
of maple that I found in an alley.
Where do you see your work going in the future?
In the November meeting for the GVWG, I demonstrated making little pill boxes. I learned so much
from that experience, and it was very rewarding to
talk with members afterwards about ideas that
were sparked. I hope to do that again sometime. I
am also thinking about another Summer Swap exchange, like the one I started last year (see the article about in the November 2024 GVWG Newsletter).
As for my own turning, I am building up a collection
of wall-mounted pieces that could eventually be a
gallery show. And I can't stop making little pill boxes, exploring form and function and trying out
scraps of various woods. I just can't stop experimenting on the lathe. It's a wonderful obsession.
You can see more of my art at https://
www.pippalattey.com/
and
on
Instagram
@pippalattey

 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 24)

Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 24
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage and GVWG Safety
webpage.
